slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by naming the shift in viewpoint. Earlier convex analysis mostly watched one function move toward minima or supporting hyperplanes. Section 33 asks students to track two directions at once: one argument is optimized like a concave variable, the other like a convex variable, and the saddle point is where both one-sided stories agree.

slides.title: Saddle Direction
slides.notes: Use the sign convention slowly. A concave-convex saddle-function bends downward in the first variable and upward in the second. The diagram is deliberately asymmetric: moving along the concave coordinate feels like maximizing, while moving along the convex coordinate feels like minimizing. That sign split is the grammar for the rest of Part VII.

slides.title: Simple Extensions
slides.notes: The first technical nuisance is domain extension. If the original function is defined only on C times D, the natural infinity outside D is plus infinity for convexity in the second variable, while the natural infinity outside C is minus infinity for concavity in the first variable. When both variables leave their domains, there is no single forced value, which is why lower and upper simple extensions appear.

slides.title: Partial Closure
slides.notes: Present closure as coordinate-wise regularization rather than a global smoothing operation. Closing in the convex variable repairs lower semicontinuity slice by slice; closing in the concave variable repairs upper semicontinuity slice by slice. The important habit is to ask which coordinate is being closed and which inequality direction that closure is supposed to protect.

slides.title: Partial Conjugacy
slides.notes: This is the central construction. Start with a convex bifunction F, freeze u, and take the ordinary conjugate of F u with respect to x. The resulting expression is convex in the dual variable x star, but Theorem 33.1 says it is also concave in u. That extra concavity is what turns a family of convex functions into a saddle-function.

slides.title: Recovering The Bifunction
slides.notes: Now reverse the construction. If a saddle-function is convex-closed in the second variable, each slice can be conjugated back to recover F u. This is the image-closed correspondence: no hidden generator is needed once the closed convex slices are known. Students should recognize the same conjugate involution idea from earlier sections, now applied only in one coordinate.

slides.title: Adjoint Equation
slides.notes: The adjoint theorem is best read as a generalized inner product identity. In linear algebra, the pairing Au with x star equals the pairing u with A star x star. For bifunctions, the two expressions may need closure before they match. The closure relation explains both the analogy and the boundary cases where the analogy is too optimistic.

slides.title: Where Equality Holds
slides.notes: Emphasize that equality is not promised everywhere. It holds on relative interiors of the appropriate domains and in the polyhedral case except for the clear double-outside exception. Near the boundary, the two partial conjugate views can disagree, become infinite in opposite directions, or reflect abnormal dual behavior. That is the bridge to the next section.

slides.title: Closedness Ladder
slides.notes: Organize the many closedness words into a small ladder. Convex-closed and concave-closed are one-coordinate properties. Fully closed means both are present. Lower closed and upper closed are weaker two-step properties that remember which coordinate should be semicontinuous in the natural direction. This ladder prevents the section from sounding like a list of nearly identical labels.

slides.title: Restricted Continuous Case
slides.notes: Use the continuous-on-C-times-D case as the sanity check. For closed convex C and D and finite continuous saddle data, the lower and upper simple extensions give the two closed representatives that the theory wants. A unique closed convex bifunction sits behind them, with domain C and adjoint domain D, so the abstract closure language returns to ordinary restricted saddle data.

slides.title: Quadratic Saddle Lab
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to the notebook artifact. The quadratic K of u and x star equals minus one half u squared plus u x star plus one half x star squared. It is concave in u and convex in x star, the partial derivatives vanish at the origin, and the saddle inequality reads K of u zero is at most K of zero zero, which is at most K of zero x star.

slides.title: Learner Checks
slides.notes: Frame the lab as a residual dashboard. The stationarity residual checks the two partial derivatives at the candidate. The concave-side inequality checks that moving u alone cannot raise the value above the center, and the convex-side inequality checks that moving x star alone cannot lower it below the center. When a parameter change breaks one residual, students should identify which side of the saddle has failed.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the vocabulary into one route. Saddle-functions are convex analysis with a sign split. Partial conjugacy turns bifunctions into saddle-functions and recovers them slice by slice. The adjoint identity is a closure-sensitive replacement for the linear adjoint pairing. Lower and upper closed representatives are the durable objects that the following minimax sections will use.
